qs.q: What is the primary pathological consequence and risk associated with untreated vesicoureteral reflux in children?
o: Conversion to squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary tract
Rapid onset of bladder exstrophy at birth
Widespread mucosal calcification resulting in stone formation
Progressive pyelonephritis leading to loss of renal function
qs.e: Vesicoureteral reflux is the most serious congenital anomaly of the bladder because it predisposes the patient to ascending pyelonephritis and subsequent loss of renal function. It does not directly cause bladder exstrophy, which is a separate structural wall defect.
qs.s: Lower Urinary Tract & Ureter Pathology: Obstruction & Tumors: MCQs

qs.q: A voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is performed on a 2-year-old girl with pyelonephritis, demonstrating contrast reflux into the ureter and renal pelvis with mild dilation and well-preserved caliceal fornices. Which grade of vesicoureteral reflux does this represent?
qs.e: Grade III VUR is defined by mild dilation of the renal pelvis and ureter without the loss of calyces. Grade II shows no dilation, Grade IV has moderate dilation with loss of calyces, and Grade V shows severe dilation with tortuosity.

qs.q: What radionuclide scan is used in the surveillance of vesicoureteral reflux to assess renal morphology, structure, and function?
qs.e: A DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is a radionuclide scan utilized to assess renal morphology, structure, and function in patients undergoing conservative management for VUR. It helps detect renal scarring.

qs.q: Which diagnostic modality is considered the gold standard to rule out vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)?
qs.e: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) uses contrast in the urinary tract to diagnose and grade vesicoureteral reflux. Ultrasound is the initial imaging study for urinary tract anomalies but MCUG rules out VUR.

qs.q: An 18-month-old girl with recurrent febrile urinary tract infections is diagnosed with low-grade vesicoureteral reflux. What is the recommended initial conservative medical management?
o: Continuous systemic corticosteroid therapy during peak infection seasons
High-dose therapeutic broad-spectrum antibiotics for six continuous months
Prophylactic antibiotics given once daily at a fraction of the full dose
Long-acting urinary alkalinizers taken three times daily after meals
qs.e: Management includes prophylactic antibiotics given once a day at 1/3 of the therapeutic dose, choosing an agent that concentrates in the urine. Surgical treatment is reserved for breakthrough infections or high grades.

qs.q: A voiding cystourethrogram is performed on a 3-year-old boy to investigate recurrent urinary tract infections, revealing contrast reflux into the renal pelvis with mild calyceal blunting. How is this grade of vesicoureteral reflux classified?
o: Severe tortuosity and massive dilation of the entire collecting system
Contrast confined strictly to the distal ureter without reaching the pelvis
Reflux into the collecting system with complete effacement of all calyces
Mild dilation of the renal pelvis and ureter without loss of calyces
qs.e: Grade III VUR represents mild dilation of the renal pelvis and ureter without loss of calyces. Grade V features severe dilation and a tortuous ureter.

qs.q: A 3-year-old girl with grade III vesicoureteral reflux and continuous antibiotic prophylaxis is evaluated in the clinic. Which finding serves as a definitive indication for surgical ureteral reimplantation?
qs.e: Breakthrough febrile urinary tract infections while compliant with prophylactic antibiotics are a primary indication for surgical ureteral reimplantation. Stable low-grade reflux without infection is managed medically with observation.

faq.a: Ultrasound shows anatomy but cannot demonstrate reflux; VCUG visualises urine flow during voiding, which is essential for grading.
faq.q: Why is VCUG still the reference test if ultrasound is easier?

faq.a: They reduce infection frequency, which lowers scarring risk, especially in low‑grade VUR; they do not eliminate the need for surveillance.
faq.q: Can low‑dose antibiotics prevent renal scarring?

faq.a: For grades III‑V with breakthrough infections, renal scarring, or when prophylaxis fails, surgical re‑implantation or endoscopic injection is recommended.

exam: A 2‑year‑old boy presents with his third febrile UTI in 6 months – what is the next investigative step and why? — VCUG to grade reflux; ultrasound alone may miss low‑grade VUR.

Explain how an oblique ureteric entry prevents reflux and why a defect leads to VUR. — The oblique tunnel creates a flap valve; a short or straight tunnel fails to close during bladder contraction, allowing backflow.

A child on prophylactic trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole develops a breakthrough UTI – what does this indicate and what is your next action? — Indicates prophylaxis failure; obtain urine culture, start targeted antibiotics, and consider surgical referral.

Differentiate primary VUR from reflux secondary to posterior urethral valves. — Primary VUR is congenital valve incompetence without obstruction; PUV shows bladder outlet obstruction, dilated posterior urethra on imaging, and often presents in neonates.
What renal changes on ultrasound suggest chronic VUR‑related damage? — Cortical thinning, echogenic scarring, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and reduced kidney size.

Why might a VCUG performed within 2 weeks of a UTI give a false‑high grade, and how would you manage this? — Inflammation makes the ureteric orifice appear more patulous; delay VCUG 2–6 weeks if the child is stable.
List three low‑resource strategies to reduce VUR complications when VCUG is unavailable. — Use serial renal ultrasound, strict infection prophylaxis, and educate caregivers on early fever detection.
What are the long‑term risks of untreated high‑grade VUR? — Progressive renal scarring, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and possible end‑stage renal failure.
ai.title: Vesicoureteral Reflux
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is the backward flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys, predisposing to recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical clues and limited imaging, while management balances infection control and preventing kidney damage.

b: Primary VUR: congenital defect of the ureterovesical junction (oblique entry, valve incompetence).
Secondary VUR: due to obstruction, neurogenic bladder, or bladder outlet obstruction.
sections.p: VUR is defined as retrograde urine passage from the bladder into the ureter(s) during voiding, confirmed by imaging that shows contrast moving upward.

t.b: Does the ureteric orifice allow reflux? – Presence and grade of reflux; gold‑standard for diagnosis.
Is there hydronephrosis, scarring, or obstruction? – Detects structural changes; normal scan does not exclude VUR.
Is there a urinary tract infection? – Positive culture confirms infection; guides antibiotic choice.

b: Grade I: reflux into non‑dilated ureter only.
Grade II: reflux into renal pelvis without dilation.
Grade III: mild ureteral and pelvic dilation.
Grade IV: moderate dilation and tortuosity.
Grade V: severe dilation, tortuosity, and loss of papillary impression.
sections.p: VUR is graded I–V on VCUG based on the extent of reflux and dilation.

b: Primary congenital ureterovesical junction incompetence (most common).
Neurogenic bladder from spina bifida or meningomyelocele.
Posterior urethral valves (boys).
Obstructive uropathy from stones or severe constipation.
Infections that scar the valve (e.g., recurrent pyelonephritis, HIV‑related kidney disease).
sections.p: Most cases are primary congenital defects; secondary causes are common in low‑resource settings.

b: Fever, dysuria, flank pain after a UTI.
Failure to thrive or growth delay in chronic cases.
Hematuria is uncommon but may appear with infection.
sections.p: Children often present with recurrent febrile urinary tract infections, but may be asymptomatic if low grade.
Imaging and labs are directed at confirming reflux, assessing renal damage, and identifying infection.

t.b: Confirms reflux and grades severity – guides need for surgical referral.
Detects hydronephrosis, scarring, or obstruction – if unavailable, rely on clinical course.
Assesses renal function – rising creatinine suggests progressive damage.
Detects infection – treat before any invasive study.

b: Recurrent febrile UTI despite prophylaxis.
Progressive renal scarring on ultrasound.
Declining renal function (elevated creatinine).
Hypertension in older children.
sections.p: Uncontrolled reflux can lead to irreversible kidney injury.

b: Acute UTI: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotic (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) pending culture; adjust when sensitivities return.
Low‑grade VUR (I‑II) in children >1 yr: continuous low‑dose prophylaxis (e.g., trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole) if infections recur.
Higher grades (III‑V) or breakthrough infections: refer for surgical correction (ureteric re‑implantation) or endoscopic injection (deflux).
Hydration and bladder training: avoid constipation, encourage regular voiding.
sections.p: Treat infection, prevent further reflux, and monitor renal health.

b: Repeat renal ultrasound every 6–12 months in grades III‑V or after any scar‑forming infection.
Annual blood pressure check and serum creatinine.
Educate caregivers on early fever detection and prompt medical review.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring aims to catch renal damage early.

b: Posterior urethral valves – obstructive, mainly in newborn boys.
Neurogenic bladder – abnormal voiding due to neurologic disease.
Obstructive uropathy from stones or congenital hydronephrosis.
sections.p: Conditions that also cause recurrent UTIs or renal scarring.

b: Normal ultrasound does not rule out low‑grade VUR.
Negative urine culture after antibiotics may be false‑negative; consider repeat culture if symptoms persist.
VCUG performed too early (within 2 weeks of infection) may over‑estimate reflux due to bladder inflammation.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever >38 °C with flank pain or dysuria
Persistent vomiting, dehydration, or reduced urine output
Rapidly rising creatinine or new hypertension
